CausalChain: FGF19-driven FGFR4 overactivation -> Enhanced tumor cell proliferation and baseline TGF-β production -> TGF-β–mediated upregulation of PD-L1 in the tumor microenvironment -> Partial restoration of immune activity upon FGFR4 inhibition alone -> Recognition of additional compensatory immunosuppressive pathways -> Synergistic antitumor response when combining FGFR4 inhibition with TGF-β blockade and PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibition
Hypothesis: In FGF19-positive HCC, selective inhibition of FGFR4 will reduce tumor proliferation and, to a moderate extent, decrease TGF-β production and subsequent PD-L1 upregulation. Nonetheless, recognizing that multiple compensatory pathways sustain immunosuppression, we further hypothesize that a strategic combination of FGFR4 inhibitors with agents that directly target TGF-β signaling, together with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade, will synergistically enhance antitumor immune responses. This combination regimen, refined and monitored in real time using next-generation multi-omic profiling and digital pathology, promises a more effective and personalized therapeutic approach to overcome immune resistance in this HCC subset.
Abstract: In FGF19‐positive hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), aberrant activation of FGFR4 drives tumor proliferation and contributes to an immunosuppressive microenvironment through multiple mechanistic pathways. Here, we propose that selective FGFR4 inhibition not only diminishes tumor cell survival signals but also partially reduces TGF‐β production, leading to a decrease in PD‐L1 expression. However, given the multifactorial regulation of the tumor microenvironment, we further hypothesize that a triple‐combination therapy—integrating FGFR4 inhibitors, targeted TGF‐β pathway antagonists, and PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockade, supported by real-time molecular profiling (e.g., multi-omic analyses and digital pathology)—will robustly overcome immune resistance in FGF19‐positive HCC. This refined hypothesis leverages advanced technological capabilities to both validate and optimize patient‐tailored immunomodulatory intervention strategies.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that selective FGFR4 inhibition could reprogram the tumor microenvironment solely through the modulation of TGF-β–mediated PD-L1 upregulation. The revised hypothesis maintains the causal chain—that FGFR4 overactivation increases TGF-β and PD-L1 levels—but acknowledges that FGFR4 inhibition only partially impacts these immunosuppressive pathways. To address the identified gaps and observed compensatory mechanisms, we incorporate direct targeting of TGF-β signaling along with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Moreover, we enhance practical implementation by integrating advanced technologies such as multi-omic profiling and digital pathology for real-time biomarker monitoring, thereby improving the precision and efficacy of the proposed combination therapy.
